Abstract

We implement merge sort sequentially and in parallel with OpenMP tasks, in two variants requested in the proposal review: the classic 2-way merge sort and a 4-way merge sort whose recursion splits every range into four quarters and merges them with a tournament tree. Both are evaluated on large arrays of 32-bit integers of up to 200M elements (1.6 GB including the scratch buffer) with 1–8 threads. On a Intel(R) Core(TM) i5-8250U CPU @ 1.60GHz (4 cores / 8 hardware threads) the best parallel run sorts 200M integers in 7.60 s (par4, 8 threads) versus 22.87 s for the best sequential version, a speedup of 3.01×. At 8 threads the 4-way variant is 22% faster. To explain these numbers we build an analytical, level-by-level performance model calibrated only with micro-benchmarks (merge/leaf throughput, task overhead); it predicts the full-sort times with a mean absolute error of 8.6% (8.8% for n ≥ 50M) without ever being fitted to them. Every output of every run was verified to be sorted and a permutation of the input.

1. Introduction and Objectives

Sorting is a building block of databases, search and scientific codes. Merge sort is naturally divide-and-conquer: the two (or four) sub-arrays at each level are independent and can be sorted concurrently, which maps directly onto OpenMP's task model. The proposal was approved with changes; this report addresses all of them:

Instructor feedback → what we did
  • 2-way merge sort — sequential baseline + OpenMP-task version (src/mergesort2.c).
  • 4-way merge sort should be there — sequential + OpenMP-task 4-way version with a tournament-tree 4-way merge (src/mergesort4.c), compared head-to-head with 2-way at every size and thread count.
  • Large array size — arrays from 1M up to 200M integers (the generator and sorts use 64-bit indices; larger sizes such as 500M/1G run unchanged on machines with enough free RAM).
  • Accurate modelling — a work/span analysis plus a calibrated analytical model that predicts run time for every (variant, n, threads, cutoff) and is validated against all measurements (Section 6).

Objectives from the proposal: (1) implement and validate sequential merge sort; (2) parallelise it with OpenMP tasks; (3) merge correctly; (4) evaluate on large arrays with different thread counts; (5) report time, speedup and efficiency with tables and graphs; (6) study the task cutoff and diminishing returns.

2. Background

2.1 k-way merge sort

A k-way merge sort splits the input into k parts, sorts them recursively and merges the k sorted runs. With leaves of size L the recursion depth is logk(n/L). Every level reads and writes the whole array once, so a 4-way sort makes half as many passes over memory as a 2-way sort (e.g. 23 vs 12 levels for n = 200M, L = 32). The price is a more expensive merge: choosing the minimum of 4 heads. With a 2-level tournament tree only the pair whose head was consumed is replayed, so a 4-way merge costs 2 comparisons per element — over half the levels, i.e. the same n·log2n total comparisons as 2-way, but with fewer memory passes and more instruction-level work per element.

2.2 OpenMP tasks

#pragma omp task packages a unit of work that any thread of the team may execute; taskwait waits for the child tasks. A recursive algorithm therefore expresses parallelism without knowing the thread count: the runtime's work-stealing-like scheduler balances the tree. Creating a task costs time (measured here: 0.03 µs with 1 thread, 3.65 µs with 8), so small sub-arrays must be handled sequentially — the task cutoff.

The project is written in C11 with OpenMP 4.5 (GCC). Source layout:

3.1 Common design decisions

  • Ping-pong buffers. One scratch array of n ints is allocated once. Each recursion level merges from one buffer into the other (a to_tmp flag alternates per level), so there is no copy-back pass and no allocation inside the sort.
  • Leaf size 32. Sub-arrays of ≤ 32 elements are finished with insertion sort, which is faster than recursing.
  • Same kernel for sequential and parallel. Below the task cutoff the parallel version calls exactly the sequential function, so the comparison measures parallelism, not different code.
  • Task cutoff (default 16,384 elements): ranges at or below it become a single task-free subtree.

3.2 Parallel 2-way merge sort

The first half is spawned as a task and the current thread recurses into the second half itself (this saves one task per node), then taskwait and merge:

static void ms2_task(int *a, int *t, size_t n, int to_tmp, size_t cutoff)
{
    if (n <= cutoff) {               /* sequential cutoff */
        ms2_rec(a, t, n, to_tmp);
        return;
    }
    size_t h = n / 2;

    #pragma omp task firstprivate(a, t, h, to_tmp, cutoff)
    ms2_task(a, t, h, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    /* the current thread works on the second half itself */
    ms2_task(a + h, t + h, n - h, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    #pragma omp taskwait

    if (to_tmp) merge2(a, h, a + h, n - h, t);
    else        merge2(t, h, t + h, n - h, a);
}

3.3 Parallel 4-way merge sort

Three quarters are spawned as tasks, the fourth is processed by the current thread:

static void ms4_task(int *a, int *t, size_t n, int to_tmp, size_t cutoff)
{
    if (n <= cutoff) {                 /* sequential cutoff */
        ms4_rec(a, t, n, to_tmp);
        return;
    }
    size_t q  = n / 4;
    size_t o1 = q, o2 = 2 * q, o3 = 3 * q;
    size_t n3 = n - o3;

    #pragma omp task firstprivate(a, t, q, to_tmp, cutoff)
    ms4_task(a, t, q, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    #pragma omp task firstprivate(a, t, q, o1, to_tmp, cutoff)
    ms4_task(a + o1, t + o1, q, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    #pragma omp task firstprivate(a, t, q, o2, to_tmp, cutoff)
    ms4_task(a + o2, t + o2, q, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    /* the current thread sorts the last quarter itself */
    ms4_task(a + o3, t + o3, n3, !to_tmp, cutoff);

    #pragma omp taskwait

    int *src = to_tmp ? a : t;
    int *dst = to_tmp ? t : a;
    merge4(src, q, src + o1, q, src + o2, q, src + o3, n3, dst);
}

The 4-way merge keeps the head of each run as a 64-bit key; an exhausted run gets the key +∞ (INT64_MAX), which no 32-bit value can equal, so the loop needs no end-of-run special cases and is correct for INT_MIN/INT_MAX:

void merge4(const int *r0, size_t n0, const int *r1, size_t n1,
            const int *r2, size_t n2, const int *r3, size_t n3, int *out)
{
    const int *p[4] = { r0, r1, r2, r3 };
    const int *e[4] = { r0 + n0, r1 + n1, r2 + n2, r3 + n3 };
    int64_t k[4];
    for (int i = 0; i < 4; i++)
        k[i] = (p[i] < e[i]) ? (int64_t)*p[i] : KEY_INF;

    int w01 = (k[1] < k[0]) ? 1 : 0;
    int w23 = (k[3] < k[2]) ? 3 : 2;

    const size_t total = n0 + n1 + n2 + n3;
    for (size_t o = 0; o < total; o++) {
        int w = (k[w23] < k[w01]) ? w23 : w01;   /* final match */
        out[o] = (int)k[w];
        p[w]++;
        k[w] = (p[w] < e[w]) ? (int64_t)*p[w] : KEY_INF;
        if (w < 2) w01 = (k[1] < k[0]) ? 1 : 0;   /* replay only one pair */
        else       w23 = (k[3] < k[2]) ? 3 : 2;
    }
}

3.4 Correctness validation

pdcsort test compares every variant element-by-element with the C library qsort on 33 sizes (0, 1, 2, around the leaf size 32, around powers of two, odd primes up to 3,000,017) × 6 input distributions (uniform, sorted, reversed, 16 distinct values, all equal, nearly sorted) × 4 thread counts × 3 cutoffs (including cutoff = 32, which creates a task for almost every node), plus INT_MIN/INT_MAX: 5,152 test cases, all passing. In the benchmarks every timed run is additionally checked to be non-decreasing and to have the same order-independent 64-bit fingerprint (sum of hashed values) as the input, proving the output is a permutation of the input.

5.3 Observations

  • Sequential: 2-way takes 25.65 s and 4-way 22.87 s for 200M elements; the 4-way version is faster by 11% (4-way was faster sequentially at 7 of 7 sizes). Calibration explains why: one pass of merge4 runs at 116M elements/s versus 197M for merge2 (1.71× slower per pass), but the 4-way sort needs only half as many passes, a net gain of about 15% in the merge phase. A branchy merge is limited by branch mispredictions rather than memory bandwidth in a single thread, so the saving comes from fewer passes, not from bandwidth.
  • Parallel: the best 2-way speedup is 2.64× (p=6) and the best 4-way speedup is 3.01× (p=8).
  • Diminishing returns: speedup grows quickly up to 4 threads (one per physical core) and much more slowly from 4 to 8 threads, because Hyper-Threads share a core's execution units: calibration shows per-thread merge2 throughput of 197M elements/s alone, 123M with 4 concurrent threads and 118M with 8 (Figure 5).
  • 2-way vs 4-way in parallel: the 4-way version was faster in 35 of 35 parallel configurations. At 8 threads and n = 200M it needs 7.60 s against 9.76 s.
  • Small arrays (1M) finish in tens of milliseconds; parallel overheads and timer resolution (~1 ms) limit speedup.

6. Performance Modelling

6.1 Work and span (theory)

Let the merge cost be c per element. The work is W = Θ(n log n) for both variants. Because each merge in our algorithm is performed by a single thread, the critical path (span) is the chain of merges from a leaf to the root:

Span2-way ≈ c2(n + n/2 + n/4 + …) ≈ 2c2n     Span4-way ≈ c4(n + n/4 + n/16 + …) ≈ (4/3)c4n

so the available parallelism W/Span = Θ(log n) is small: the top-level merge alone touches all n elements on one thread, an Amdahl-type serial bottleneck. Using the calibrated rates, the span for n = 200M is T∞ = 2.03 s (2-way) and 2.31 s (4-way), so even with infinitely many threads the speedup cannot exceed about 12.9× (2-way) or 9.9× (4-way). The 4-way tree has a shorter span in merge steps (4n/3 vs 2n), but each step of a 4-way merge is slower.

6.2 Calibrated level-by-level model

The recursion is modelled as d = ⌈logk(n/C)⌉ merge levels above the cutoff C plus one leaf phase. Level i contains M = ki independent merges of size s = n/ki; at most q = min(p, M) threads can work on it:

T(n,p) = ⌈kd/qd⌉·L / rleaf(k,qd,L) + Σi=0d-1 ⌈Mi/qi⌉· si / rmerge(k,qi,si) + Ntasks·ttask(p)/p

The throughputs r(k, q, s) are measured by pdcsort calibrate: q threads simultaneously run k-way merges (or leaf sorts) of size s on private buffers. This single table captures the three effects that make the naive “T1/p” estimate wrong: cache effects (small merges fit in L2/L3), shared DRAM bandwidth, and Hyper-Threading contention (per-thread throughput falls when q > 4). The model never sees a full-sort timing; it is a genuine prediction.

6.3 Model accuracy

Mean absolute percentage error: 8.6% over all runs ≥ 0.1 s, 8.8% for n ≥ 50M; 79% of predictions are within ±15%. Figure 7 shows why speedup saturates: at p = 8 the top levels, which have fewer merges than threads, account for a large share of the run time even though they are a small share of the work. 6.4 Where the model deviates: task scheduling in the 2-way tree

Broken down by case, the mean error is 1.5% / 1.4% for the sequential 2-way / 4-way sorts, 8.3% for 2-way with 1–2 threads, 7.1% and 8.6% for 4-way with < 4 and ≥ 4 threads, but 14.5% for 2-way with ≥ 4 threads, where the measured time is consistently longer than predicted. The model assumes greedy scheduling: whenever a level has M ≥ p ready merges, all p threads are busy. Our 2-way code spawns one half as a task and lets the parent thread continue with the other half. When the parent finishes its half first, it blocks in taskwait for the sibling that another thread is running. In GCC's OpenMP runtime (libgomp), a thread waiting in taskwait executes only its own child tasks, not unrelated ready tasks; if none of its children is still queued, the thread sleeps. With a binary tree and 4+ threads, many such waits overlap. The 4-way tree reaches 4 independent subtrees after one split and 16 after two, so threads are rarely starved, and the model fits it well.

To test this explanation we ran an alternative 2-way version that spawns both halves as tasks (pdcsort variants). A waiting parent can then execute one of its own children instead of idling:

Threads12468
2-way, spawn 1 + continue (s)5.9343.3932.7362.5992.332
2-way, spawn both (s)5.9123.1212.2312.2161.761
4-way (s)5.3183.0591.9762.0631.723

Spawning both halves moves the 2-way times towards the model at ≥ 4 threads, which supports the explanation. We kept the “spawn one + continue” form as the main implementation because it is the textbook form described in the proposal, and because this comparison is itself a useful result: how tasks are spawned matters as much as how many. The 4-way design avoids the problem by construction.

7. Task Cutoff Analysis

The best cutoff was 1,048,576 for 2-way (2.303 s) and 8,192 for 4-way (1.808 s). With the smallest cutoff (32 elements, i.e. a task for nearly every node) millions of tasks are created. Time rises to 4.25 s (2-way) and 7.05 s (4-way): task creation and scheduling, about 3.7 µs per task on 8 threads, now costs more than the work inside the task. 4-way suffers more because it creates 3 tasks per node. Above that, the curve is remarkably flat: every cutoff from 128 to 4,194,304 (2-way) and 2,048 to 1,048,576 (4-way) is within 10% of the best. A large cutoff such as 4M still leaves 50M/4M ≈ 16 leaf tasks, enough for 8 threads, but begins to cost load balance. We use 16,384 elements (64 KB, which fits in the 256 KB L2 cache), safely inside the flat region.

8. Discussion

  • 2-way vs 4-way. 4-way won 35 of 35 parallel configurations. It needs half the passes over memory, has a shorter critical path in merge steps (4n/3 vs 2n), and creates parallelism faster: 4 independent subproblems after one split instead of 2. That avoids the idle-thread effect of Section 6.4. Its merge costs more instructions per element, but fewer passes more than make up for it on this machine.
  • Why speedup is far below p. (1) The sequential top merges (span); (2) only 4 physical cores — threads 5–8 are Hyper-Threads; (3) shared memory bandwidth (26 GB/s) is split between the cores during the lower merge levels; (4) thermal/turbo limits of a laptop CPU when all cores are busy.
  • Model insights. The model is accurate because it is built from the same kernels under the same contention, level by level. Its largest error (2-way, ≥ 4 threads) is not noise: it exposes a runtime-scheduling effect (threads idling in taskwait) that a greedy-scheduling model cannot see (Section 6.4). Smaller remaining errors come from turbo-frequency variation and background load.
  • Improvement beyond this project. The top-level bottleneck can be removed with a parallel merge (split both runs by binary search and merge the pieces in parallel), giving span O(log3 n); a branch-free merge kernel would also raise per-thread throughput.

9. Conclusion

We implemented, validated and analysed sequential and OpenMP task-parallel 2-way and 4-way merge sorts on arrays of up to 200M integers; every benchmark output was verified correct. The best configuration achieved 3.01× speedup over the best sequential sort on a 4-core/8-thread CPU. A calibrated level-by-level model predicted the run times within 8.6% on average and explains the diminishing returns: the serial top-level merges and Hyper-Threading, not task overhead, limit scalability once the task cutoff is chosen sensibly.
